title: Audit, quality improvement & risk
blurb: Clinical governance, the audit cycle, written protocols, risk assessment, incident reporting and significant event analysis.
question: Your practice manager asks you to lead an audit of radiograph quality after several images had to be retaken. Last month there was also a near miss when the wrong patient's tray was set up. How would you run the audit properly, and what should the team do about the near miss?

teach.h: Clinical governance: keeping care safe and improving
teach.body: Clinical governance is the framework a practice uses to make sure care is safe and keeps getting better. It includes audit, risk assessment, incident reporting, written protocols, staff training, patient feedback and good records. It also covers the quality of what reaches the patient, such as checking that lab work matches the prescription and that equipment is serviced. In England, the CQC inspects against five key questions: is the service safe, effective, caring, responsive and well-led? The GDC lists monitoring, auditing and contributing to clinical governance as part of a dental nurse's role.

teach.caption: Re-auditing closes the loop: it shows whether your changes actually worked.

teach.body: Audit asks "are we meeting the standard we agreed?" Research asks a new question to create new knowledge. An audit measures what you do now, compares it with a standard taken from guidance, makes changes and then measures again. Common dental audits include radiograph quality, infection control, record keeping and hand hygiene. Clinical audit can also count as verifiable CPD if it meets the GDC's evidence requirements.

items.label: decontamination audit at least this often (HTM 01-05)

teach.caption: Radiographs are graded A (diagnostically acceptable) or N (not acceptable) under the 2020 guidance notes.

teach.body: Written protocols should be based on current national guidance and the practice's own risk assessment. Writing them down means everyone works the same way and practice can be checked. If two nurses use different decontamination routines, instruments may not be processed safely. Protocols must be reviewed regularly, or they drift out of date. Records prove what happened: if nobody recorded this week's sterilizer checks, instruments may have been released without verified cycles. Audit results and records reviewed over time are the best evidence that a system works.

A risk assessment looks at what could cause harm in the practice and what you are doing to prevent it. It covers things like sharps, chemicals, radiation, manual handling and slips. The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) describes five steps. The aim is not to remove every risk, but to reduce each one as far as is reasonably practicable and to write down what you have done.

teach.h: HSE's five steps to risk assessment
teach.caption: HSE's current wording is: identify hazards, assess the risks, control the risks, record your findings, review the controls. The steps are the same.

teach.h: Incidents, near misses and significant event analysis
teach.body: A near miss is an event that could have caused harm but didn't. Report incidents and near misses factually: what happened, when, who was involved and what was done, without opinion or blame. In a significant event analysis (SEA) the team meets to work out what happened, why, what was learned and what will change. It focuses on fixing the system. Incidents that are recorded but never reviewed tend to happen again. Simple checks, such as confirming the patient's identity, prevent wrong-patient treatment.

teach.caption: Some events must also be reported outside the practice, for example under RIDDOR or to the MHRA for a faulty device or medicine.

teach.text: An audit isn't finished once you've measured. Without making changes and re-auditing, the cycle isn't closed and you can't show improvement.

items: Audit cycle: topic, standard, measure, compare, change, re-audit.
Audit checks practice against a standard; research creates new knowledge.
Protocols: based on national guidance and risk assessment, written down, reviewed regularly.
Missing records mean you can't prove something was done, such as sterilizer checks.
Risk assessment: identify, who's harmed, evaluate, record, review.
Report incidents factually; use SEA to fix systems, not blame people.

summary: You can now explain clinical governance, run a full audit cycle including re-audit, tell audit from research, explain why protocols must be written, current and followed consistently, carry out the five steps of risk assessment, and report and learn from incidents and near misses.

A.q: You are asked to complete a hand hygiene audit. What is the purpose of the audit cycle?
options: To measure, change practice and re-measure
To find out which nurse to discipline
To produce new research for a journal
To replace the written infection control policy
A.why: The audit cycle measures practice against a standard, makes changes and then re-measures to check improvement.

whyNot.1: Audit is about improving systems, not disciplining individuals.
whyNot.2: Audit checks against an existing standard; research creates new knowledge.
whyNot.3: Audit tests how well policy is followed; it doesn't replace it.

A.q: Two nurses in the practice follow different decontamination routines. What is the main risk?
options: One nurse will always finish earlier
Patients may notice the difference
Instruments may not be processed safely
The sterilizer will wear out faster than usual
A.why: Inconsistent routines mean some instruments may not be processed to the required standard.

whyNot.0: Timing is a minor issue compared with patient safety.
whyNot.1: Patients are unlikely to see decontamination; the risk is to their safety.
whyNot.3: Equipment wear isn't the main concern.

A.q: After a near miss with the wrong instrument tray, the practice holds a team meeting. What is the main purpose?
options: To identify exactly who was to blame
To find what allowed it and fix the system
To decide whether to issue a written warning
To agree that it doesn't need recording
A.why: Discussing near misses as a team identifies the system weaknesses that allowed them, so they can be fixed.

whyNot.0: Blame discourages reporting and doesn't fix the system.
whyNot.2: Significant event discussions are about learning, not discipline.
whyNot.3: Near misses should be recorded so the learning isn't lost.

B.q: There is no record of who carried out this week's sterilizer checks. What is the risk?
options: The CQC will close the practice on the same day
The sterilizer warranty will be void
There is no risk if it seemed to work
Instruments may have been released unverified
B.why: Without test records, there is no proof the sterilizer was working, so instruments may have been released without verified cycles.

whyNot.0: Inspection action isn't instant; the real risk is to patients.
whyNot.1: Warranty isn't the concern; patient safety is.
whyNot.2: "Seeming to work" is not evidence that sterilisation was achieved.

B.q: You are asked to help write a new practice protocol. What should it be based on?
options: What the last practice manager preferred
National guidance and a risk assessment
Whatever is quickest for the busy team
The product manufacturer's sales brochure
B.why: Protocols should reflect current national guidance and the practice's own risk assessment.

whyNot.0: Personal preference isn't a sound basis for safe practice.
whyNot.3: Sales material may be biased; national guidance comes first.

B.q: Which detail is most important to include in an incident report?
options: A factual account of what happened and when
Your own opinion of who caused it
A note of how annoyed you felt at the time
A request to keep it from the rest of the team
B.why: Incident reports should be factual: what happened, when, who was involved and what action was taken.

whyNot.1: Opinions and blame make reports less reliable.
whyNot.2: Feelings belong in personal reflection, not the factual report.
whyNot.3: Incidents should be shared so the team can learn.

C.q: How does clinical audit differ from research?
options: Audit always needs ethics approval
Research is only done in dental practices
Audit checks practice against a standard
There is no difference between them
C.why: Audit measures current practice against an agreed standard; research generates new knowledge.

whyNot.0: Clinical audit doesn't usually need research ethics approval.
whyNot.1: Research takes place in many settings.
whyNot.3: They have different aims and methods.

C.q: The practice's decontamination policy hasn't been reviewed for four years. Why does this matter?
options: Policies legally expire after three years
It will be too short to be useful
The CQC only accepts typed policies
It may no longer reflect current guidance
C.why: Guidance and equipment change, so policies must be reviewed regularly to stay current.

whyNot.0: There is no fixed legal expiry, but regular review is expected.
whyNot.1: Length isn't the issue; being out of date is.
whyNot.2: Format isn't the concern; content is.

C.q: A colleague never checks the patient's identity before treatment starts. What is the main risk?
options: The appointment may overrun
Treatment on the wrong patient
The patient may feel rushed
The notes may be filed late
C.why: Identity checks prevent the wrong patient receiving treatment, X-rays or medication.

whyNot.0: Timing is a minor issue compared with wrong-patient treatment.
whyNot.2: Feeling rushed isn't the main risk of skipping ID checks.
whyNot.3: Filing is unrelated to identity checks.

reteach.title: Audit is like checking your bank balance
reteach.question: You set yourself a monthly food budget. How do you find out whether you're sticking to it, and what do you do if you're not?

blocks.h: Set it, check it, fix it, check again
blocks.body: You decide on a budget (the standard). You look at your statement (measure). You compare what you spent with the budget. If you overspent, you change something, like planning meals. Then you check again next month to see if it worked. That last check is the bit people forget, and it's exactly what re-audit is.

explain.body: Choose a topic, set a standard, measure, compare, make changes, then re-audit. Re-audit shows whether the changes worked.

test.q: In the audit cycle, what should happen after changes have been made?
options: The audit is filed away and closed
The standard is lowered to match the results
Practice is re-audited against the standard
The staff involved are disciplined
test.why: Re-auditing checks whether the changes improved practice.

whyNot.0: Closing without re-audit leaves the loop open.
whyNot.1: Lowering the standard hides the problem.
whyNot.3: Audit is about improving systems, not punishment.

explain.body: Written protocols keep practice consistent and checkable. Records and audit results over time are the evidence that systems work.

test.q: What provides the best evidence that the practice's infection control is effective?
options: Audit results and records kept over time
Staff saying they follow the policy
No patient complaints this year
The surgery looking clean
test.why: Audit results and records reviewed over time give objective evidence that systems work.

whyNot.1: What staff say isn't objective evidence.
whyNot.2: A lack of complaints doesn't prove infection control works.
whyNot.3: Looking clean doesn't prove instruments are sterile.

explain.body: Identify hazards, decide who might be harmed and how, evaluate risks and decide precautions, record the findings, then review and update.

test.q: What is the final step of a risk assessment?
options: Identify the hazards
Record the findings
Decide who might be harmed
Review and update it
test.why: Risk assessments must be reviewed and updated regularly and after any change.

whyNot.0: Identifying hazards is the first step.
whyNot.2: Deciding who might be harmed is the second step.

explain.body: Report incidents and near misses factually. Use significant event analysis to understand why it happened and fix the system. Unreviewed incidents recur.

test.q: The practice records incidents but never reviews them. What is the likely consequence?
options: Staff will report more incidents
The same failures are likely to recur
The incidents will resolve themselves
Patients will be better protected
test.why: Without review, the causes aren't fixed, so the same failures tend to happen again.

whyNot.0: Staff usually stop reporting if nothing changes.
whyNot.2: Problems don't fix themselves without action.
whyNot.3: Patients are only protected if lessons lead to change.
